title: Diseases of Hypersensitivity
subject: Immune System (IMMU)

overview.intro: Hypersensitivity is an adaptive immune response that injures the host. This chapter uses the Gell and Coombs classification as a set of four mechanisms: IgE and mast cells (type I), antibody against fixed cell or matrix antigens (type II), deposited immune complexes (type III), and T cells (type IV). Each disease is taught from its mechanism, so that timing, tissue distribution, serology, complement levels, and immunofluorescence pattern can be predicted rather than memorized. Board questions usually give a vignette and ask for the mechanism, the expected laboratory or biopsy finding, or the type of reaction, and real diseases often combine more than one type.
prerequisites: Antibody classes and their effector functions (complement fixation, Fc receptor binding)
Complement pathways, C3a and C5a, opsonization, and the membrane attack complex
CD4 T helper subsets (Th1, Th2, Th17), CD8 cytotoxic T cells, and their cytokines
MHC class I and II and the basis of self tolerance
Glomerular structure and the nephritic syndrome

connections.how: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia and drug-induced hemolysis are read with the direct Coombs test, the smear, and markers of red cell destruction.
Linear, granular, and pauci-immune immunofluorescence patterns separate anti-GBM disease, immune complex glomerulonephritis, and ANCA vasculitis.
The safety factor of neuromuscular transmission explains why myasthenia gravis weakness is fatigable.
Group A Streptococcus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Epstein-Barr virus, hepatitis B, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis each trigger a hypersensitivity disease in this chapter.
Rheumatoid synovitis and lupus arthritis show how immune injury in the joint can be erosive or nonerosive.

terms.def: An adaptive immune response, against a foreign or self antigen, that is excessive or misdirected and damages tissue.
The first exposure to an antigen that produces the antibodies or memory T cells that cause injury on later exposure.
Exocytosis of preformed mediators such as histamine and tryptase from mast cell or basophil granules.
Coating of a target by IgG or C3b so that phagocytes with matching receptors bind and remove it.
A test in which anti-human globulin added to washed patient red cells causes agglutination if the cells are coated with IgG or C3; also called the direct antiglobulin test.
A lattice of antigen bound to antibody that can fix complement and deposit in vessels, glomeruli, and synovium.
A proliferation of parietal epithelial cells and macrophages with fibrin in Bowman space, marking severe glomerular injury.
A focal aggregate of activated (epithelioid) macrophages, often with multinucleated giant cells and a lymphocyte rim, that walls off persistent antigen.
Cheese-like central necrosis of a granuloma that leaves amorphous granular debris, typical of tuberculosis.
A small molecule, such as a penicillin metabolite, that becomes immunogenic only after it binds a host protein.
Vessel wall injury in which deposited immune complexes, plasma proteins, and fibrin give a bright pink smudged appearance.

sections.title: Type I hypersensitivity: IgE and mast cells

blocks.text: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity is a reaction of preformed IgE bound to mast cells and basophils. It needs two exposures. During sensitization, dendritic cells present the allergen to naive CD4 T cells, which in an atopic host differentiate into Th2 cells. Th2 cells secrete IL-4 and IL-13, which, together with CD40 ligand on the T cell, switch B cells to IgE production; IL-5 matures and activates eosinophils. Free IgE has a serum half-life of only a few days, but once it binds the high-affinity Fc epsilon receptor I (FcepsilonRI) on mast cells, it can arm them for weeks to months.

On re-exposure, a multivalent allergen bridges two or more adjacent IgE molecules. Cross-linking clusters FcepsilonRI, activates tyrosine kinases, and raises cytosolic Ca2+. Monovalent antigen cannot do this, which is why cross-linking, not binding, is the trigger. Three classes of mediator follow. Preformed granule contents (histamine, tryptase, heparin) are released within seconds to minutes. Membrane phospholipid yields arachidonic acid, which 5-lipoxygenase converts to leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 and cyclooxygenase converts to prostaglandin D2 over minutes. Cytokines (TNF, IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) are transcribed over hours.

blocks.text: The immediate phase peaks within about 5 to 30 minutes. Histamine acting on H1 receptors dilates arterioles, opens endothelial gaps in postcapillary venules, contracts bronchial and gut smooth muscle, and stimulates sensory nerves (itch). Leukotrienes are far more potent and longer-acting bronchoconstrictors and also increase permeability and mucus secretion. The late phase begins about 2 to 8 hours later and can last a day: cytokines and chemokines recruit eosinophils, Th2 cells, basophils, and neutrophils, and eosinophil granule proteins (major basic protein) damage epithelium. The late phase explains why allergic asthma persists after the initial bronchospasm and why repeated reactions cause chronic airway remodeling.

blocks.text: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, systemic, potentially fatal type I reaction in which antigen reaches mast cells in many tissues at once. The common triggers are foods (peanut, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, egg), Hymenoptera venom (bee, wasp, fire ant), drugs (penicillins and other beta-lactams), and natural rubber latex. Penicillin is too small to be immunogenic alone; its breakdown product, the benzylpenicilloyl group, binds host proteins covalently as a hapten and creates the epitope that IgE recognizes. The same picture can occur without IgE when agents such as iodinated contrast, opioids, or vancomycin activate mast cells directly; this is still anaphylaxis clinically but is not a type I reaction.

Each sign follows from a mediator effect. Dermal venular leak produces urticaria (raised, itchy wheals), and leak in the deeper dermis and submucosa produces angioedema of the lips, tongue, and larynx, giving hoarseness and stridor. Leukotrienes and histamine contract bronchial smooth muscle, causing wheeze and dyspnea. Generalized arteriolar dilation and capillary leak, which can shift a large fraction of plasma volume out of the circulation within minutes, cause distributive shock with tachycardia and hypotension. Gut smooth muscle contraction causes cramping, vomiting, and diarrhea. Onset is usually within minutes of injected or stung antigen and within about 2 hours of ingestion, and some patients have a second (biphasic) reaction hours later without new exposure.

blocks.text: Serum tryptase confirms mast cell activation after the fact. Histamine peaks within minutes and is cleared within about an hour, so it is rarely captured. Tryptase peaks about 1 to 2 hours after onset and has a half-life of about 2 hours, so blood drawn roughly 15 minutes to 3 hours after onset is most useful, compared with a baseline drawn at least 24 hours after recovery. A commonly used rule counts a rise as significant when the acute value exceeds 120% of baseline plus 2 ng/mL. A normal tryptase does not exclude anaphylaxis, because food-induced reactions, especially in children, often involve less mast cell tryptase release. A persistently high baseline (above about 11 ng/mL) points to a mast cell disorder such as systemic mastocytosis or to hereditary alpha-tryptasemia.

blocks.title: Interpreting a tryptase rise
blocks.text: A woman develops hives, wheeze, and a blood pressure of 78/40 mm Hg ten minutes after a wasp sting. Tryptase drawn 90 minutes after onset is 14 ng/mL; her baseline, drawn a week later, is 5 ng/mL. The threshold is 1.2 times 5 plus 2, which is 8 ng/mL. Her acute value of 14 ng/mL exceeds it, so the episode involved systemic mast cell degranulation, consistent with venom anaphylaxis. Her baseline is normal, so a mast cell disorder is not suggested. If the acute value had been 7 ng/mL, the rise would not reach the threshold, but the clinical diagnosis would still stand, because tryptase is specific for mast cell activation but not fully sensitive.

sections.title: Warm and cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia

blocks.text: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) is a type II reaction in which autoantibody binds antigens on the patient's own red cells. The antibody class decides the temperature at which it binds, whether it fixes complement, and where the red cells are destroyed. Both forms share the general signs of hemolysis: anemia, reticulocytosis, raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH, and low haptoglobin. Both are proven by a positive direct Coombs test (direct antiglobulin test), in which anti-human globulin added to washed patient red cells agglutinates them if IgG or C3 is already on their surface.

Warm AIHA, the more common form, is caused by IgG (usually IgG1 or IgG3) that binds best at 37 °C (98.6 °F), often to Rh-related membrane proteins. IgG fixes complement weakly, so coated cells are not lysed in the circulation. Instead, splenic macrophages bind them through Fc gamma receptors and remove pieces of membrane. A red cell that loses membrane without losing volume becomes a spherocyte, which is rigid and is trapped and destroyed in the splenic cords. This is extravascular hemolysis, and the spleen enlarges. About half of cases are idiopathic; the rest accompany SLE, chronic lymphocytic leukemia and other lymphomas, or drugs. Spherocytes with a positive Coombs test separate warm AIHA from hereditary spherocytosis, which is Coombs negative.

Cold agglutinin disease is caused by IgM, which binds red cells best at about 0 to 4 °C (32 to 39 °F) and still binds in the cooler blood of the fingers, toes, ears, and nose. Pentameric IgM agglutinates red cells, causing acrocyanosis in the cold, and fixes C1 strongly. When the blood returns to the warm core, IgM detaches, but C3b remains, so the Coombs test detects C3 rather than IgG. Kupffer cells in the liver remove C3b-coated cells, and some cells proceed to the membrane attack complex and lyse in the vessels, causing hemoglobinuria. Secondary cases follow Mycoplasma pneumoniae (anti-I antibody) and Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis (anti-i), are polyclonal, and resolve within weeks. Chronic primary disease reflects a clonal B cell disorder that makes monoclonal IgM. Agglutinates on the smear can also produce a falsely high MCV on automated counters.

blocks.text: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease is a type II reaction against a structural antigen. IgG autoantibodies bind the noncollagenous (NC1) domain of the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen. This chain is concentrated in the glomerular basement membrane and the alveolar basement membrane, which explains why the kidney and lung are the two targets. In the intact collagen network the epitope is partly hidden, and an injury that exposes it is thought to allow antibody access. Susceptibility is strongly linked to HLA-DR15. Goodpasture syndrome refers to the combination of glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage; some patients have kidney disease alone.

Bound IgG activates complement and engages Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages, which release proteases and oxidants that break the basement membrane. Fibrin and plasma proteins then leak into Bowman space, and parietal epithelial cells and infiltrating macrophages proliferate into crescents that compress the glomerular tuft. When crescents involve most glomeruli, filtration falls over days to weeks, which is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), presenting as a nephritic syndrome with hematuria, red cell casts, proteinuria, and rising creatinine. Because the antigen is a continuous sheet, immunofluorescence shows smooth linear IgG along the capillary walls rather than the lumpy granular deposits of immune complexes.

blocks.text: The alveolar basement membrane is normally shielded by tight alveolar endothelium, so lung hemorrhage occurs mostly when it is injured, especially in cigarette smokers and after inhaled hydrocarbons or infection. Bleeding into the alveoli causes hemoptysis, diffuse infiltrates, hypoxemia, iron deficiency anemia, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the sputum or lavage. The disease has a bimodal pattern: younger men often present with the pulmonary-renal form, and older adults more often with kidney disease alone. Serum anti-GBM antibody supports the diagnosis, and a minority of patients are also positive for MPO-ANCA.

blocks.text: Myasthenia gravis is a type II reaction in which antibody impairs the function of a receptor without killing the muscle fiber, which is why it is called noncytotoxic. In about 85% of generalized cases, IgG binds the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) on the postsynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction. These antibodies act in three ways: they fix complement and damage the tips of the junctional folds, they cross-link receptors and speed their internalization and degradation, and some block the acetylcholine binding site. Fewer receptors and simplified folds mean that each quantum of acetylcholine produces a smaller end-plate potential. A smaller group has IgG4 antibodies to muscle-specific kinase (MuSK), which does not fix complement but disrupts the clustering of AChRs.

Normal transmission has a safety factor: the end-plate potential is several times larger than needed to reach threshold. During sustained activity, acetylcholine release per impulse falls as the readily releasable vesicle pool is depleted. Healthy junctions tolerate this, but in myasthenia the reduced end-plate potential drops below threshold in more and more fibers, so strength fades with use and recovers with rest. Repetitive nerve stimulation at about 3 Hz shows a decremental compound muscle action potential for the same reason.

Extraocular muscles and the levator palpebrae are affected first in most patients, giving ptosis and diplopia that worsen late in the day; their high firing rates and low safety factor are the usual explanation. Generalized disease adds proximal limb weakness, bulbar weakness (dysarthria, dysphagia, nasal speech), and in a crisis respiratory failure. Sensation and reflexes are preserved, and the pupils are spared because the iris muscles are autonomically controlled smooth muscle, which lacks the skeletal muscle nicotinic receptor. Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase prolongs acetylcholine in the cleft and transiently improves strength, consistent with a shortage of functional postsynaptic receptors.

The thymus is central. Thymic myoid cells express AChR, and thymic follicular hyperplasia with germinal centers is found in most young patients with AChR antibodies. About 10 to 15% of patients have a thymoma, and a substantial minority of patients with thymoma develop myasthenia. MuSK-positive disease rarely shows thymic pathology.

blocks.title: Myasthenia gravis versus Lambert-Eaton syndrome
blocks.caption: The side of the junction that is attacked decides whether activity worsens or improves strength.

blocks.predict: A patient has drooping eyelids that worsen through the day, normal pupils, and normal reflexes. Why are the pupils spared?
blocks.explain: The antibodies target the nicotinic receptor of skeletal muscle. Pupil size is set by autonomically controlled smooth muscle (muscarinic sphincter, adrenergic dilator), which lacks that receptor, so pupils remain normal.

sections.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus: pathogenesis and serology

blocks.text: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic autoimmune disease driven by autoantibodies to nuclear antigens. Most of its tissue injury is type III (immune complex deposition), while its cytopenias are type II (antibody against blood cells). The central defect is loss of tolerance to nuclear material that is normally hidden or quickly removed.

Apoptotic cells are normally cleared by phagocytes before they release their contents, with help from opsonins such as C1q. In SLE this clearance is impaired. Inherited deficiency of early classical complement components carries a high risk of lupus (over 90% with C1q deficiency, lower with C4 and C2), which shows that complement protects against autoimmunity as well as causing injury. Ultraviolet light increases keratinocyte apoptosis, explaining photosensitivity. Persisting DNA, nucleosomes, and ribonucleoproteins bind antibody, and the complexes are taken up by plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells through Fc receptors and B cell receptors. Inside endosomes, self RNA engages TLR7 and self DNA engages TLR9, driving type I interferon production and activating autoreactive B cells. Female sex hormones, genes such as HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3, and some drugs add to risk. Complexes deposit in glomeruli, skin, joints, serosa, and vessel walls, activate complement, and recruit neutrophils and macrophages.

blocks.text: Serology rests on the difference between sensitivity and specificity. The antinuclear antibody (ANA) by immunofluorescence is positive in about 95% or more of patients, so a negative ANA makes SLE very unlikely, but it is also positive in other autoimmune diseases and in many healthy people at low titer. Anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies are highly specific, so a positive result supports the diagnosis. Anti-dsDNA titers rise with disease activity and nephritis; anti-Smith does not track activity. Anti-histone antibodies are found in nearly all cases of drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid), which typically has arthritis and serositis but spares the kidney and brain, lacks anti-dsDNA, and resolves when the drug is stopped. Anti-histone is also common in idiopathic SLE, so it is useful only in that setting.

Flares consume complement through the classical pathway, so C3 and C4 fall and rise again with remission. Falling complement with rising anti-dsDNA is the classic signal of active nephritis. The ESR is often raised in flares, whereas the CRP is often only mildly raised unless serositis or infection is present.

sections.title: Manifestations of SLE and antiphospholipid syndrome

blocks.text: SLE affects women about nine times as often as men, usually between puberty and menopause, and it is more frequent and more severe in women of African, Hispanic, and Asian ancestry. The typical vignette is a young woman with fatigue, fever, joint pain, and a rash after sun exposure.

blocks.title: Manifestations of SLE and their mechanisms
rows: Malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds; photosensitivity; discoid scarring lesions
UV-induced apoptosis; immune complexes at the dermal-epidermal junction
Synovitis without pannus; deformities are reducible
Type II antibodies to blood cells
Antibodies, cytokines, and small vessel injury
blocks.caption: Most features are immune complex injury; cytopenias are direct antibody attack on cells.

blocks.text: Lupus nephritis is the most important predictor of outcome. Immune complexes deposit in the mesangium, beneath the endothelium (subendothelial), or beneath the podocytes (subepithelial), and the site determines the pattern. Subendothelial deposits are in contact with circulating blood, so they provoke the most inflammation and cause proliferative nephritis with a nephritic picture. Large subendothelial deposits thicken capillary walls so that they look rigid and bright on light microscopy, the wire loop lesion of diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis. Immunofluorescence is granular, often with IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q together (a full house pattern). Subepithelial deposits cause membranous lupus nephritis with nephrotic syndrome. Libman-Sacks endocarditis consists of small sterile vegetations on either surface of the leaflets, most often the mitral valve; they can scar the valve or embolize.

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) occurs alone or with SLE. Its antibodies are directed against phospholipid-binding plasma proteins, chiefly beta2-glycoprotein I, and are measured as lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I. In the test tube, lupus anticoagulant interferes with the phospholipid surface of clotting assays and prolongs the aPTT, yet in the body the antibodies activate endothelium, platelets, monocytes, and complement and cause thrombosis. Clinical events are venous thrombosis (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism), arterial thrombosis (stroke), and pregnancy morbidity from placental thrombosis and complement-mediated trophoblast injury: recurrent early losses, fetal death, or early preeclampsia. Anticardiolipin can also give a false-positive nontreponemal syphilis test (VDRL, RPR), because that test uses cardiolipin as its antigen. The antibody must be persistent, on testing at least 12 weeks apart.

blocks.predict: A woman with SLE has a prolonged aPTT and a recent deep vein thrombosis. How can a test that suggests poor clotting coexist with thrombosis?
blocks.explain: The prolonged aPTT is a laboratory artifact: the antibodies bind the phospholipid surface the assay depends on. In the body, the same antibodies activate endothelium, platelets, and complement, favoring clot formation.

blocks.text: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, the main visceral arteries and their branches. It spares arterioles, capillaries, and venules, so it does not cause glomerulonephritis, and it characteristically spares the pulmonary arteries, so the lungs are not involved. It is not associated with ANCA, which separates it from the small vessel vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. Middle-aged adults are affected most often.

A subset of cases is caused by chronic hepatitis B infection, in which complexes of hepatitis B surface antigen and antibody deposit in arterial walls, fix complement, and recruit neutrophils. This is the basis for classifying PAN as a type III disease. Hepatitis B vaccination has made this association much less common, and most current cases have no identified trigger. Hairy cell leukemia is a rare association.

The lesion is segmental and transmural. In the acute phase, neutrophils, eosinophils, and mononuclear cells infiltrate the whole wall, and fibrinoid necrosis replaces it. Later the wall heals with fibrosis. Because new lesions keep appearing, acute and healed lesions are seen side by side in the same patient and even in the same vessel; this mixture of stages is a distinguishing feature of PAN. Necrosis weakens the wall, producing small aneurysms, and thrombosis or fibrotic narrowing occludes the lumen, producing infarcts. Angiography of the renal and mesenteric arteries shows multiple microaneurysms and stenoses (a beaded pattern).

blocks.text: Diagnosis relies on biopsy of an affected organ, such as nerve, muscle, or skin, showing necrotizing arteritis, or on angiographic microaneurysms. Hepatitis B serology is part of the evaluation because it identifies the cause.

Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is an immune complex nephritis that follows infection with certain nephritogenic strains of group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). It occurs about 1 to 4 weeks after the infection: roughly 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis and closer to 3 to 6 weeks after skin infection (impetigo). This latent period is the time needed to make antibody, which separates PSGN from IgA nephropathy, in which hematuria appears within a day or two of a mucosal infection. Children of about 5 to 12 years are most often affected.

Streptococcal antigens, chiefly the cationic proteinase streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (SpeB) and the nephritis-associated plasmin receptor, lodge in the glomerulus, where antibody binds them in situ; circulating complexes also deposit. The complexes activate complement mainly through the alternative pathway, so serum C3 is low while C4 is usually normal or only mildly low. C3 returns to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks; persistently low C3 suggests another diagnosis, such as lupus nephritis or C3 glomerulopathy.

Complement and neutrophils make the glomeruli enlarged and hypercellular (diffuse proliferative and exudative glomerulonephritis). Electron microscopy shows large subepithelial deposits called humps, and immunofluorescence shows granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls and in the mesangium. Inflamed capillaries leak red cells and reduce filtration, producing the nephritic syndrome: smoke or cola colored urine with red cell casts, mild to moderate proteinuria, oliguria, periorbital edema, and hypertension. Sodium and water are retained because the GFR falls while tubular reabsorption continues. Recent infection is shown by antistreptolysin O (ASO), which rises after pharyngitis, or anti-DNase B, which is the better marker after skin infection because skin lipids inactivate streptolysin O and blunt the ASO response. Most children recover fully; adults recover less reliably.

blocks.title: Hematuria after a sore throat
blocks.text: Two patients have cola colored urine and red cell casts. Patient A, aged 8, had a sore throat 2 weeks earlier, has periorbital edema and hypertension, a low C3, a normal C4, and a high ASO. Patient B, aged 22, noticed the hematuria 1 day after the onset of a sore throat and has a normal C3. Patient A fits PSGN: the 2 week delay allowed antibody production, and immune complexes consumed C3 through the alternative pathway. Patient B fits IgA nephropathy: hematuria appears almost at once, mesangial IgA deposits do not lower serum complement, and biopsy would show mesangial IgA rather than subepithelial humps. If patient A still had a low C3 at 3 months, the diagnosis of PSGN should be questioned.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune synovitis that destroys cartilage and bone. It affects about 0.5 to 1% of adults, women about three times as often as men, usually starting between 30 and 50 years. Its injury is driven mainly by T cells, macrophages, and cytokines, with a contribution from immune complexes in the joint and in extra-articular lesions; this is why it appears under type III in many lists, although it combines types III and IV.

Susceptibility is strongest with HLA-DRB1 alleles that share a common amino acid sequence (the shared epitope), especially HLA-DR4. Peptidyl arginine deiminase enzymes convert arginine in proteins to citrulline, a process increased by smoking in the lung. HLA-DR4 binds citrullinated peptides well, presenting them to CD4 T cells, which then help B cells make anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA, measured as anti-CCP). These antibodies can appear years before arthritis. In the synovium, Th1 and Th17 cells, B cells, and plasma cells accumulate, and macrophages release TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. Synovial fibroblasts proliferate and, with new vessels and inflammatory cells, form pannus, which invades cartilage at the joint margins. RANKL on T cells and fibroblasts activates osteoclasts, producing marginal erosions and periarticular osteopenia.

blocks.text: The arthritis is symmetric and involves the small joints of the hands (MCP and PIP joints), the wrists, and the MTP joints, while sparing the DIP joints, which are typical targets of osteoarthritis and psoriatic arthritis. Morning stiffness lasting more than about an hour improves with use. Later deformities include ulnar deviation, swan neck, and boutonniere deformities, and cervical C1 to C2 instability. Rheumatoid factor is an antibody, usually IgM, against the Fc portion of IgG; it is positive in most patients but also in hepatitis C, Sjogren syndrome, chronic infections, and healthy older adults. Anti-CCP is slightly less sensitive but far more specific (about 95%) and predicts erosive disease. Rheumatoid nodules form over pressure points such as the extensor forearm and consist of central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading macrophages; they occur mainly in seropositive patients. Felty syndrome is seropositive, long-standing RA with splenomegaly and neutropenia, which predisposes to bacterial infection. Other extra-articular features include interstitial lung disease, pleural effusion with low glucose, scleritis, vasculitis, and secondary AA amyloidosis.

sections.title: Type IV hypersensitivity and granulomatous inflammation

blocks.text: Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity is injury caused by T cells rather than antibody. CD4 T cells act through cytokines: Th1 cells activate macrophages and Th17 cells recruit neutrophils. CD8 T cells kill antigen-bearing cells directly. Memory T cells must be recruited to the site and activated before injury appears, so the reaction peaks about 48 to 72 hours after exposure.

A granuloma is the Th1 response to an antigen that macrophages ingest but cannot destroy, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which survives inside phagosomes. Infected macrophages and dendritic cells secrete IL-12, which drives naive CD4 T cells to become Th1 cells. Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages: phagolysosome fusion improves, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species increase, and MHC class II rises. Activated macrophages enlarge, gain abundant pink cytoplasm, and resemble epithelial cells (epithelioid cells), and some fuse into multinucleated giant cells, including Langhans giant cells with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe. TNF from macrophages and T cells induces chemokines and adhesion molecules that keep recruiting monocytes and hold the granuloma together. When TNF is blocked, granulomas break down and latent tuberculosis can reactivate, and inherited defects in IL-12 or IFN-gamma signaling cause severe mycobacterial infection.

blocks.caption: The granuloma contains the antigen at the cost of tissue destruction and scarring.

blocks.text: Granulomas are divided by whether the center is necrotic. Caseating granulomas have central caseous necrosis, an amorphous granular pink debris, and are the classic lesion of tuberculosis; endemic fungi such as Histoplasma also cause them. Noncaseating granulomas lack central necrosis and occur in sarcoidosis, Crohn disease, berylliosis, and reactions to foreign material. A caseating granuloma should always prompt a search for mycobacteria or fungi with special stains and culture.

The tuberculin skin test is a small, deliberate type IV reaction. Purified protein derivative (PPD) is injected into the dermis; a person with memory Th1 cells to mycobacterial antigens develops induration at 48 to 72 hours as T cells and macrophages accumulate. Only induration, not redness, is measured in millimeters. A positive test means prior sensitization (latent or active infection, or BCG vaccination); it does not distinguish latent from active disease. False negatives occur when T cell function is impaired (anergy), as in advanced HIV, sarcoidosis, high-dose glucocorticoids, overwhelming miliary tuberculosis, or very recent infection.

blocks.caption: The cutoff falls as the pretest probability of infection or the risk of progression rises.

blocks.text: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem disease of noncaseating granulomas of unknown cause. It is thought to reflect an exaggerated Th1 and Th17 response to an unidentified antigen in a genetically susceptible host. It usually begins between 20 and 40 years, with a second peak in older women, and in the United States it is more common and more severe in Black women. CD4 T cells concentrate in the lungs, giving a high CD4 to CD8 ratio in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, while blood lymphocytes fall. This redistribution helps explain the cutaneous anergy seen on skin testing.

The lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes are involved in more than 90% of patients. Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest imaging is the classic finding, with or without reticular lung opacities; lung disease causes cough, dyspnea, a restrictive pattern, and reduced diffusing capacity, and it can progress to fibrosis. The granulomas are tight and well formed; giant cells may contain asteroid bodies or Schaumann bodies, but these inclusions are not specific.

Two laboratory findings arise from granuloma macrophages. Epithelioid cells produce angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), so serum ACE is often raised and roughly reflects granuloma burden; it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose sarcoidosis. Activated macrophages also express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without control by PTH. Calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption, causing hypercalciuria (more common) and hypercalcemia with a suppressed PTH, which can worsen after sun exposure.

blocks.title: Extrapulmonary sarcoidosis
rows: Anterior uveitis (red, painful eye, blurred vision)
Erythema nodosum (tender red nodules on the shins); lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on nose and cheeks)
Conduction block, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death
Facial nerve palsy, other cranial neuropathies
blocks.caption: Erythema nodosum is a nonspecific panniculitis; lupus pernio signals chronic disease.

blocks.text: Lofgren syndrome is an acute presentation with erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and arthritis, typically of the ankles, often with fever. It carries a good prognosis, and most patients remit spontaneously within about 2 years. Because noncaseating granulomas have other causes, sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion: tuberculosis and fungal infection must be excluded with stains and cultures, and beryllium exposure considered.

Rejection is an immune response against donor alloantigens, mainly the highly polymorphic MHC (HLA) molecules, and against ABO antigens on vascular endothelium. Recipient T cells recognize donor MHC in two ways. In direct recognition, donor dendritic cells carried in the graft present intact foreign MHC, which activates an unusually large fraction of recipient T cells and drives acute cellular rejection. In indirect recognition, recipient antigen-presenting cells process donor MHC into peptides, which helps B cells make donor-specific antibody and sustains chronic rejection. Timing reflects mechanism.

blocks.title: Types of rejection
rows: Preformed antibody (ABO, anti-HLA from pregnancy, transfusion, prior graft); type II
Complement on endothelium, thrombosis, ischemic necrosis; graft turns dusky and mottled
Days to months, mostly first months
CD8 T cells kill graft cells; CD4 cytokines; type IV
Repeated T cell and antibody injury to vessels
Graft arteriosclerosis, interstitial fibrosis, organ-specific scarring
blocks.caption: Preformed antibody acts at once; T cells must first expand; chronic injury accumulates in vessels.

blocks.text: Chronic rejection is the main cause of late graft loss. Smooth muscle cells proliferate in the intima of graft arteries, producing concentric narrowing (graft arteriosclerosis) and ischemic fibrosis. Its form depends on the organ: interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy in the kidney, accelerated diffuse coronary disease in a heart graft (often silent because the heart is denervated), bronchiolitis obliterans with progressive airflow obstruction in a lung graft, and loss of bile ducts in a liver graft.

Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) reverses the direction of attack. Immunocompetent donor T cells in a graft rich in lymphocytes, usually a hematopoietic stem cell transplant, recognize host tissues as foreign. The host must be unable to reject those cells, because of conditioning or immunodeficiency. Acute GVHD targets epithelia: the skin (a maculopapular rash, often starting on the palms and soles, that can progress to blistering), the liver (cholestatic jaundice from bile duct injury), and the gut (watery or bloody diarrhea from crypt cell apoptosis). Chronic GVHD resembles autoimmune disease, with sclerodermatous skin, dry eyes and mouth, and obliterative bronchiolitis. The same donor T cells can attack residual leukemia, the graft-versus-leukemia effect.

blocks.predict: A woman with three prior pregnancies receives a kidney, and within minutes after the vascular clamps are released the graft becomes mottled and soft. What caused this?
blocks.explain: Pregnancy exposed her to paternal HLA, so she had preformed anti-HLA antibodies. They bound graft endothelium at once, activated complement, and caused thrombosis: hyperacute rejection, a type II reaction.

sections.title: Serum sickness and the Arthus reaction

blocks.text: Serum sickness is the model systemic type III reaction. It was first described after injections of horse serum antitoxin and now follows foreign proteins such as antithymocyte globulin and chimeric monoclonal antibodies. Its course follows the changing ratio of antigen to antibody. A large dose of antigen circulates, and after about 5 to 7 days antibody production begins. While antigen is still in moderate excess, small and intermediate complexes form; these fix complement but are poorly cleared by mononuclear phagocytes, so they deposit in vessel walls, glomeruli, and synovium. Complement fragments, especially C5a, attract neutrophils, whose enzymes cause vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, and arthritis.

blocks.title: Course of serum sickness
steps: Large dose of foreign protein

Complexes deposit in vessels, glomeruli, synovium
Complement consumed; C5a recruits neutrophils
Fever, rash, arthralgia, proteinuria
Antigen cleared; symptoms resolve
blocks.caption: Symptoms appear when antibody first meets abundant antigen and fade when antigen is gone.

blocks.text: Symptoms begin about 1 to 2 weeks after first exposure, or within a few days in someone already sensitized. Fever, urticarial or morbilliform rash, arthralgia or arthritis, lymphadenopathy, and proteinuria are typical, and C3 and C4 are low because complement is consumed. The illness resolves over weeks as antigen is cleared and antibody excess forms large complexes that phagocytes remove.

The Arthus reaction is the local form. When antigen is injected into the skin of a person who already has high levels of IgG, complexes form within the walls of local small vessels. Complement activation and neutrophil influx cause a localized necrotizing vasculitis with edema, hemorrhage, and sometimes ulceration, peaking at about 4 to 12 hours. Overly frequent tetanus or diphtheria toxoid boosters are a classic cause. The timing separates it from a type I wheal, which appears in minutes, and from a type IV reaction, which takes 48 to 72 hours.

Drugs cause all four types of hypersensitivity. Most drugs are too small to be antigens, so they act as haptens: the drug or a reactive metabolite binds a host protein covalently, and the drug-protein conjugate is recognized as foreign. Which type results depends on whether the immune response is dominated by IgE, IgG against cells, circulating complexes, or T cells, and on where the antigen sits. Penicillin is the classic example of a single drug that can cause more than one type.

Drug induces true autoantibody to red cell antigens; warm AIHA
Serum sickness from chimeric monoclonal antibodies or antithymocyte globulin

Hapten binds skin proteins; Langerhans cells prime T cells
blocks.caption: One drug can cause different reactions depending on the immune response it provokes.

blocks.text: The two type II hemolytic patterns differ in a testable way. With penicillin, antibody recognizes the drug on the red cell membrane, so hemolysis requires high drug levels and stops when the drug is withdrawn; the direct Coombs test is positive for IgG. With methyldopa, the drug alters immune regulation so that the patient makes autoantibodies against red cell antigens themselves. A positive direct Coombs test is common in long-term users, but hemolysis develops in only a small fraction, and the antibody can persist for months after the drug is stopped.

In contact dermatitis, the hapten penetrates the skin and binds epidermal proteins; Langerhans cells carry it to regional lymph nodes and prime T cells during sensitization. On re-exposure, effector T cells return to the skin and cause a pruritic, eczematous, often vesicular eruption sharply limited to the area of contact. Nickel and urushiol from poison ivy act the same way. Reactions that mimic allergy without immune memory, such as direct mast cell activation by vancomycin or iodinated contrast, are not true hypersensitivity, and they can occur on the first exposure.

integration.text: The four types are mechanisms, not diseases, and most diseases combine them. Lupus uses type III injury in the kidney and type II injury to blood cells; rheumatoid arthritis combines T cell synovitis with immune complexes; transplant rejection can be type II (hyperacute, antibody-mediated) or type IV (acute cellular). The useful questions are where the antigen is (fixed on a cell or matrix, circulating, or inside macrophages), which effector is active (IgE, IgG or IgM with complement, or T cells), and how long the response takes. These answers predict the biopsy: linear IgG for a matrix antigen, granular deposits for immune complexes, and granulomas or lymphocytic infiltrates for T cell injury.

The laboratory follows the same logic. Complement falls when immune complexes or complement-fixing antibodies consume it (SLE flares, PSGN, serum sickness, cold agglutinin disease) but not in type I or type IV reactions. Microbes link pathology to microbiology: group A Streptococcus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, hepatitis B, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis each cause a disease in this chapter through the host response rather than direct tissue invasion. The classification has limits: some antibody-mediated diseases, such as myasthenia gravis and Graves disease, alter receptor function instead of destroying cells, and some type IV reactions are mediated by CD8 cytotoxic T cells rather than cytokine-activated macrophages.

summary: Type I: Th2 IL-4 and IL-13 switch B cells to IgE, which arms mast cells; multivalent allergen cross-links IgE and releases histamine and tryptase in minutes, with leukotrienes and an eosinophil late phase hours later.

Anaphylaxis is systemic mast cell activation causing urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, and distributive shock; serum tryptase peaks at 1 to 2 hours and supports the diagnosis but can be normal in food reactions.
Warm AIHA is IgG at 37 °C (98.6 °F) with splenic removal and spherocytes; cold agglutinin disease is IgM fixing C3 in cool extremities after Mycoplasma or EBV; both are direct Coombs positive.

Anti-GBM disease targets the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen, giving linear IgG, crescentic RPGN, and alveolar hemorrhage; myasthenia gravis antibodies remove or block AChR, causing fatigable ocular and proximal weakness linked to the thymus.
SLE results from impaired clearance of apoptotic nuclear material; ANA is sensitive, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific, anti-histone suggests drug-induced lupus, and C3 and C4 fall in flares.

Lupus features include malar rash, nonerosive arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, wire loop nephritis, and Libman-Sacks endocarditis; antiphospholipid antibodies prolong the aPTT but cause thrombosis and pregnancy loss.
PAN is an ANCA-negative, hepatitis B-linked necrotizing arteritis of medium arteries with lesions of different ages and renal and mesenteric microaneurysms, sparing the lung and glomeruli.

PSGN follows group A strep after a 1 to 4 week delay, with low C3, high ASO or anti-DNase B, subepithelial humps, and granular immunofluorescence; RA is HLA-DR4 and anti-CCP associated pannus that erodes MCP, PIP, and wrist joints and spares the DIPs.

Th1 IFN-gamma and TNF build granulomas: caseating in tuberculosis, noncaseating in sarcoidosis, where macrophage calcitriol causes hypercalcemia; the tuberculin test is read as induration at 48 to 72 hours.

Hyperacute rejection is preformed antibody in minutes, acute rejection is T cell or antibody attack over weeks to months, chronic rejection is vascular and fibrotic, and GVHD is donor T cells attacking host skin, liver, and gut.

verify: Placement of rheumatoid arthritis under type III follows the NPLEX condition list; most references describe it as mainly T cell mediated with an immune complex contribution. Confirm how NABNE expects it classified.
The tryptase rule (acute value above 120% of baseline plus 2 ng/mL) and the baseline upper limit of about 11.4 ng/mL vary with laboratory and consensus statement.
Latent periods for PSGN (about 1 to 3 weeks after pharyngitis, 3 to 6 weeks after impetigo) and the time for C3 to normalize (about 6 to 8 weeks) differ slightly between sources.
Antibody frequencies (AChR antibodies in about 85% of generalized myasthenia, thymoma in about 10 to 15%, ANA in about 95% or more of SLE) are consensus estimates that vary among cohorts.
The proportion of PAN cases related to hepatitis B has fallen with vaccination; older sources give about 30%, current series much less.
Tuberculin skin test cutoffs follow CDC guidance; confirm the current categories NABNE uses.

Antiphospholipid syndrome and SLE classification criteria were revised in 2023 (ACR and EULAR); confirm which criteria NABNE uses before testing on specific thresholds such as the number of pregnancy losses.
Some sources reserve cold agglutinin disease for the primary clonal disorder and call infection-associated cases cold agglutinin syndrome; confirm the expected terminology.
